html:
The Greek kings of Bactria, in what is now northern Afghanistan and its neighbours, struck coins from about 250 BCE that are among the finest portraits of the ancient world. They show the kings' faces in sharp, lifelike detail, often in a helmet or an elephant scalp headdress, with Greek gods on the back.

The kingdom began when Diodotus I, a governor for the Seleucid Empire, broke away around 250 BCE. Kings like Euthydemus I and Eucratides I followed. Eucratides struck the largest gold coin known from antiquity, a 20 stater piece now in Paris. The coins are also the main record: many kings are known only from them.

Greek kings who crossed the Hindu Kush (the Indo-Greeks) made their coins bilingual, Greek on one side and Prakrit in Kharosthi script on the other, sometimes square in the Indian style. The nomad rulers who took Bactria, and later the Kushans, copied the model for centuries. The Greek city at Ai-Khanoum was sacked about 145 BCE, and the kingdom fell to nomads around 130 BCE.
